17.1.crux: The Moon has no light of its own; it reflects sunlight, and as it goes round the Earth we see different amounts of its lit half: the phases of the Moon.

cards.title: Phases of the Moon

steps.text: A thin sliver appears and grows (waxing).
Half of the disc is bright.
A thin sliver, then the next new moon.

say: The changing shapes of the bright part of the Moon are called phases of the Moon.
From one full moon to the next takes a little more than 29 days.

cards.title: Why the shape changes

steps.text: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon
The Moon goes round the Earth
We see different amounts of the lit half from Earth

say: The Moon doesn't change shape: we just see more or less of its sunlit side.
cards.remember: The Moon reflects sunlight; phases come from our changing view.

cards.title: The Moon's surface
say: The Moon's surface is dusty and barren.

cards.title: Visiting the Moon

steps.text: On 21 July 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to land on the Moon
We always see the same side of the Moon from Earth

say: The Moon turns once on its axis in the same time it takes to go round the Earth, so the same side always faces us.

crux_points: The Moon reflects sunlight; it has no light of its own.
Phases (new moon to full moon and back) happen as we see different parts of its lit half.
The Moon has no air or water; Neil Armstrong landed there in 1969.

quiz.why: The Moon has no light of its own; it reflects light from the Sun.

quiz.q: The night with no Moon in the sky is called…
quiz.why: On new moon night the Moon's lit side faces away from us.

17.2.crux: Stars are like the Sun but very far away; they seem to move from east to west because the Earth spins, and their huge distances are measured in light years.

cards.title: The Sun is a star

cols.head: The Sun
cells: Light takes about 8 minutes to reach us

cols.head: Other stars
cells: Their light takes years to reach us

say: Stars give out their own light, like the Sun.
Stars are in the sky during the day too, but sunlight is too bright to see them.

cards.title: Light year

parts.text: Speed of light: 300,000 km per second

say: A light year is the distance light travels in one year. It measures distance, not time.
Alpha Centauri, a nearby star, is about 4.3 light years away.

cards.title: Why stars seem to move

steps.text: The Earth spins from west to east
So stars appear to move from east to west
The Pole Star lies along the Earth's axis, so it seems to stay still

say: The Pole Star (Dhruv tara) is above the North Pole and helps us find the north.

crux_points: Stars give out their own light; the Sun is the nearest star.
A light year is the distance light travels in one year.
Stars seem to move east to west because the Earth spins west to east; the Pole Star seems fixed.

quiz.q: A light year is a unit of…
quiz.why: It's the distance light travels in a year.

quiz.q: Why does the Pole Star seem not to move?
options: It lies along the Earth's axis
quiz.why: It is in line with the axis around which the Earth spins.

17.3.crux: Constellations are groups of stars that form recognisable shapes; well-known ones are Ursa Major, Orion and Cassiopeia.

cards.title: Famous constellations

labels.name: Ursa Major (Saptarshi)
labels.note: Seven bright stars; seen in summer evenings

labels.name: Cassiopeia
labels.note: A 'W' shape in the northern sky

say: Ancient people joined bright stars into shapes and gave them names.

cards.title: Finding the Pole Star

steps.text: Find Ursa Major in the northern sky
Join the two pointer stars at the end of its bowl
Extend the line about five times: you reach the Pole Star

say: Travellers used this to find the north at night.
cards.remember: Ursa Major's pointers lead to the Pole Star.

cards.title: When to look
say: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is near Orion.

crux_points: A constellation is a group of stars forming a recognisable shape.
Ursa Major's pointer stars lead to the Pole Star.
Orion (with its belt) and Cassiopeia (a W) are seen in winter.

quiz.why: Cassiopeia looks like a W (or a distorted M).

quiz.q: Which stars help us find the Pole Star?
options: The pointer stars of Ursa Major
quiz.why: A line through the two pointer stars leads to the Pole Star.

17.4.crux: The solar system is the Sun and everything that goes round it, including eight planets that move in fixed paths called orbits.

cards.title: Eight planets
say: Each planet moves round the Sun in its own path, called an orbit.
Pluto was once called a planet, but since 2006 it is called a dwarf planet.

cards.title: Revolution and rotation

cols.head: Rotation
cells: One spin on its own axis

say: The time for one revolution is the planet's period of revolution.
cards.remember: Revolve = go round the Sun. Rotate = spin.

cards.title: Planet facts

items.sub: Closest to the Sun; no moon
Brightest planet; 'morning or evening star'; spins east to west
Only planet known to have life; one moon
So big about 1300 Earths could fit inside

say: Uranus and Neptune are so far away we need a telescope to see them.

cards.title: Inner and outer planets
say: The asteroid belt separates the inner and outer planets.

crux_points: The solar system is the Sun and all bodies that revolve around it.
There are eight planets, from Mercury (nearest) to Neptune (farthest).
Planets revolve round the Sun in orbits and rotate on their axes.

quiz.why: Jupiter is the biggest planet, just beyond the asteroid belt.

quiz.q: Which planet is nearest to the Sun?
quiz.why: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun.

quiz.q: Which planet is known as the red planet?

17.5.crux: Besides planets, the solar system has asteroids, comets and meteors, and people have launched artificial satellites round the Earth.

cards.title: Comets

labels.name: Tail
labels.note: Always points away from the Sun

say: Comets go round the Sun in very long, stretched orbits.
Halley's comet appears about every 76 years; it was last seen in 1986.
cards.remember: A comet's tail always points away from the Sun.

cards.title: Asteroids, meteors, meteorites

items.name: Asteroids
items.eg: Small rocky bodies between Mars and Jupiter

items.name: Meteors
items.eg: Burn up in our air: 'shooting stars'

say: A meteor heats up from friction with the air and burns, leaving a bright streak.

cards.title: Artificial satellites
say: Satellites made by people go round the Earth, much closer than the Moon.
India's satellites include Aryabhata, INSAT, IRS, Kalpana-1 and EDUSAT.

cards.title: Busting a myth

cols.head: Fact
cells: Comets are natural members of the solar system and cause no disasters

say: Science helps us replace fear with understanding.

crux_points: Asteroids orbit between Mars and Jupiter.
Comets have long orbits and tails that point away from the Sun.
Meteors burn up in the air; artificial satellites serve weather, communication and remote sensing.

quiz.q: Which way does a comet's tail point?
quiz.why: A comet's tail always points away from the Sun.
Meteors heat up and burn as they enter the air.
